IN THE MATTER of disciplinary proceedings against
DR Y of X, Medical Practitioner
BEFORE THE HEALTH PRACTITIONERS DISCIPLINARY TRIBUNAL
HEARING in Dunedin on 3-4 December 2013
TRIBUNAL: Mr B A Corkill QC, Chairperson
Ms M Taylor-Cyphers, Dr A Humphrey, Dr J Kimber and

APPEARANCES: Mr A Martin and Ms H Cook, for the Director of Proceedings
Mr H Waalkens QC, for the practitioner

2
Introduction:
1. On 6 September 2013, a charge was laid against Dr Y which alleged that on or about
10 March 2009:
1.1. He breached sexual boundaries in the doctor/patient relationship during a
consultation that morning,
1.2. and at his patient's place of employment later that day,
such conduct amounting to professional misconduct.
2. Prior to the hearing, the following non-publication orders were made by consent:
2.1. a permanent order preventing the publication of the name and identifying
features of the patient involved, Ms E;1
2.2. [ ]
2.3. an interim order preventing the publication of the names and identifying
features of Dr Y.2
Legal principles:
3. The burden of proof was on the Director.
4. The appropriate standard of proof is the civil standard, that is proof to the satisfaction
of the Tribunal on the balance of probabilities, rather than the criminal standard. The
degree of satisfaction called for will vary according to the gravity of the allegations.
The greater the gravity of the allegations the higher the standard of proof: Z v
Complaints Assessment Committee [2007] 1 NZLR 65 [26]-[28] and [37].
5. Section 100 of the HPCA Act defines the grounds on which a health practitioner may
be disciplined. The Tribunal has now had ample opportunity to consider the test for
professional misconduct under the section, and the approach to it is well settled –
examples of the correct approach are found in Nuttall;3 Aladdin4 and Dale.5
1 574/Med13/258D
2 575/Med13/258D
3 8/Med04/03
4 2/Den05/04 and 13/Den04/02D
5 20/Nur05/09D

3
6. The section provides that malpractice and/or negligence and/or conduct likely to bring
discredit to the profession can constitute professional misconduct.
7. “Malpractice” is defined in the Collins English Dictionary (2nd ed) as:
1. “The immoral, illegal or unethical conduct or neglect of professional
duties. Any instance of improper professional conduct.”
8. In the new shorter Oxford English Dictionary (1993 edition) the word is defined as:
“Law. Improper treatment or culpable neglect of a patient by a physician or of a
client by a lawyer … 2 gen criminal or illegal action: wrongdoing, misconduct.”
9. Malpractice, although often equated with negligence, is perhaps better considered a
broader concept, capable of encompassing neglect, but also of extending to
trespassory conduct in the process of caring for patients in relation to consent,
breaches of patient confidence and fiduciary obligations, and other forms of conduct
reaching the necessary level of gravity, such as assaulting a patient, swearing at or
threatening a patient, a deliberate failure to obey an instruction or sexual misconduct.6
10. Negligence and malpractice were discussed by Gendall J in Collie v Nursing Council
of New Zealand7. His Honour said:
“Negligence or malpractice may or may not be sufficient to constitute
professional misconduct and the guide must be standards applicable by
competent, ethical and responsible practitioners and there must be behaviour
which falls seriously short of that which is to be considered acceptable and not
mere inadvertent error, or oversight or for that matter carelessness.”
11. Similarly, it is for the Tribunal to decide whether the conduct, if established, would be
likely to bring discredit on the medical profession. In the same case Gendall J stated:
“To discredit is to bring harm to the repute or reputation of the profession.
The standard must be an objective standard for the question to be asked by the
Council whether reasonable members of the public, informed and with the
knowledge of all the factual circumstances, could reasonably conclude that the
reputation and good standard of the nursing profession was lowered by the
behaviour of the nurse concerned.”
6 See para 23.65, “Medical Law in New Zealand”, 2006
7 [2000] NZAR 74

4
12. In IRG v Professional Conduct Committee of the Psychologists Board,8, the Court of
Appeal emphasised that the intention in enacting section 100 in its current form was to
move away from an approach that differentiated between levels of seriousness in the
charge. The differentiation was now likely to be reflected in the penalty, not the
charge.9
13. There are two steps involved in assessing what constitutes professional misconduct:
13.1. The first step involves an objective analysis of whether or not the health
practitioner’s acts or omissions can be reasonable regarded by the Tribunal as
constituting:
• malpractice; or
• negligence; or
• otherwise meets the standard of having brought, or was likely to bring
discredit to the practitioner’s profession;
13.2. The second step requires the Tribunal to be satisfied that the health
practitioner’s acts or omissions require a disciplinary sanction for the purposes
of protecting the public and/or warrant maintaining professional standards
and/or punishing the health practitioner.
14. This approach to the assessment of professional misconduct under the statute is well
established under previous decisions of the Tribunal, and in authorities such as
McKenzie v MPDT & Anor.10 In that decision, the Court stated:
"[71] In summary, the test for whether a disciplinary finding is merited is a
two stage test based on first, an objective assessment of whether the
practitioner departed from acceptable professional standards and
secondly, whether the departure was significant enough to attract
sanctions for the purposes of protecting the public. However, even at
that second stage it is not for the disciplinary tribunal or the Court to
become engaged in a consideration of or to take into account subjective
consideration of the personal circumstances or knowledge of the
particular practitioner. The purpose of the disciplinary procedure is
8 [2009] NZAR 563
9 At [49]
10 [2004] NZAR 47

5
the protection of the public by the maintenance of professional
standards. That object could not be met if in every case the Tribunal
and the Court was required to take into account subjective
considerations relating to the practitioner."
15. The correct approach to threshold is that described in the Court of Appeal in
F v Medical Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal,11 which endorsed the earlier
statement of Elias J in B v Medical Council.12 She made the important point that the
threshold is “inevitably one of degree”. The Court of Appeal expressed the issue in
this way:
“In cases of both professional misconduct and conduct unbecoming it will be
necessary to decide if there has been a departure from acceptable standards
and then to decide whether the departure is significant enough to warrant
sanction.”
16. In determining whether the departure is significant enough there must be positive
reasons to justify such a conclusion.
17. The Tribunal accepts and applies the above principles in this case.
The hearing:
18. Dr Y accepted that the charge brought against him amounted to professional
misconduct on his part and that a disciplinary finding was warranted against him.13
19. However, the charge did not particularise the specifics of the conduct involved. The
Tribunal was told that an attempt had been made to agree a summary of facts which
would have obviated the necessity of evidence being led. However agreement could
not be reached.
20. Accordingly, the Director led evidence from Ms E, the complainant. She was
described as a health practitioner that had been provided with medical services by
Dr Y during 2008 and early 2009 at [XX] and then at the [XY]. She gave details of
her recollection of the consultation which occurred on 10 March 2009 with Dr Y at
11 [2005] 3 NZLR 774
12 Noted at [2005] 3 NZLR 810
13 Brief para 2

6
the [XY], and later that day at a meeting between the two at her office. She also
described the events leading up to her complaint.
21. For the practitioner, evidence was led from:
21.1. Dr Y, who described the background events, the details of what occurred at the
consultation on 10 March 2009 and at the meeting at Ms E's office. He also
referred to the subsequent events including the imposition of conditions on his
scope of practice by the Medical Council in late 2012.
21.2. Dr C D B Wisely, who is a psychiatrist consulted by Dr Y in October 2010.
He gave evidence of the psychotherapy which had been provided since that
time the purpose of which was to deal with stress he was suffering
professionally and personally.
21.3. [ ]
Chronology:
22. The chronology of events is as follows.
23. Relevant dates are:
23.1. Dr Y obtained an MBChB at [ ].
23.2. From November 2006 to June 2008, Dr Y worked as a general practitioner
locum at [XX], [XX] working for Dr P.
23.3. In early 2008, Ms E consulted Dr Y regarding acute hearing difficulties in one
ear, which caused her stress at work. He was empathetic regarding her
circumstances which included discussion as to a past stressful event. She was
referred to a specialist for the ear complaint. Ms E consulted Dr Y on two
further occasions at [xx].
23.4. In mid 2008, Dr Y left [XX} and commenced working at [XY] (XY).
23.5. In late 2008, Ms E decided to continue with Dr Y as her GP, because she did
not want to repeat her health issues to another GP. Her main concerns
continued to be an ear complaint and depression. She made an appointment to

7
see him at the XY, having established from XX that he was no longer working
there. She saw him in late 2008, and in January and February 2009. In the
course of these consultations Ms E told Dr Y about additional life stressors she
was facing – a 10 year relationship breakup and financial stress.
23.6. 10 March 2009: Ms E attended Dr Y at the XY. He prescribed Citalopram on
a repeat basis. Although there is some common ground between the two
parties as to what then occurred, because of the way in which evidence
emerged at the hearing it will be necessary to analyse these events more fully
below. In summary, Dr Y accepts that his conduct during the consultation was
unacceptable.
23.7. Later that day, Dr Y went to Ms E's work address. There was a further
incident on which the parties again gave somewhat differing accounts which is
analysed below. Again, Dr Y accepted that his conduct on this second
occasion was inappropriate.
23.8. In 2010, prior to August, Ms E saw an "intern" at XX; in the course of this
consultation she became upset when she unexpectedly spoke about what
occurred when consulting Dr Y in the previous year.
23.9. In August 2010, Ms E made an appointment to see Dr P. Dr P had become
aware of the March 2009 issues, and asked Ms E whether she wished to take
the matter further – she said she did not. Ms E subsequently learned that Dr P
then informed Dr S (of XY) as to the events which had occurred.
23.10. On Sunday 26 September, Dr S contacted Ms E and spoke to her about these
events. Ms E was initially concerned about an apparent breach of her privacy.
As a result she stated that she did not wish the matter to be taken further.
However, she subsequently met with Dr S and discussed what had occurred.
As a result he lodged a complaint about Dr Y on 8 October 2010.
23.11. Subsequently, Dr Y became aware a complaint had been made. He telephoned

8
Ms E and they agreed to meet at a café. They discussed what had occurred in
March 2009. Ms E felt Dr Y was not contrite. For his part Dr Y recalled that
he apologised for what happened and said that Ms E was perfectly entitled to
complain. The next day Ms E telephoned Dr Y and made it clear to him she
had been very uncomfortable indeed with what occurred.
23.12. At about the same time, Dr Y consulted Dr Wisley suffering depression and
anxiety.
23.13. In 2012, Ms E formally lodged a complaint as to the March 2009 events. The
Medical Council then conducted a full investigation into the matter which
resulted in conditions being placed on Dr Y's scope of practice on
10 September 2012.
23.14. In March 2013, following an investigation by the Health and Disability
Commissioner and the issuing of a provisional opinion recommending an
apology, Dr Y wrote to Ms E acknowledging that he had failed to maintain
professional boundaries. He said he was very sorry for this.
10 March 2009 - the two accounts:
24. The evidence relating to the events of 10 March 2009 emerged before the Tribunal in
a very unusual way.
25. Ms E said in summary:
25.1. At the consultation at the XY, and after a discussion regarding depression, life
stressors, her ear complaint and the prescribing of anti-depressant medication,
Dr Y asked if he could hug her. She agreed. She presumed this was
empathetic and altruistic in nature due to the issues which she had previously
described to him. She said that as a health professional she was comfortable
with this.
She said that Dr Y then went over to the door and locked it and then shut the

9
office blinds. She said she did not feel "ok" with this and was quite shocked.
He then asked her to bend over the bed which she did. He started to perform
thrusting motions, pushing his pelvis into her backside. She said she was quite
numb.
He then stopped and told her there had been a breach of the professional
relationship and that he would need to write this in the notes. He did not tell
her she needed to transfer to another doctor. He asked where she worked and
whether he could come to see her at work. She agreed because her workplace
office was always busy with people around. She was upset, but flattered at the
request.
25.2. Later on 10 March, Dr Y arrived at her office and seemed "very hot and
nervous." He talked to one of her colleagues and they then sat down in her
office. He went and closed her office door. She was not happy with this but
did not say or do anything. She said that he then undid his trousers and asked
her to "suck" him. She said she could see his penis which was erect. He lay
down. He said words to the effect "you can suck me or I can suck you" and
told her that they could have a relationship. He said he wanted to have sex and
asked where they could go. She asked him to stop, to pull up his trousers and
sit down. She remonstrated with him and he then left. Her perception was that
Dr Y had experienced an intense need to have sex. Ms E said that she did not
recall Dr Y asking whether there was somewhere they could go, but
acknowledged that she had a family member who had a bach nearby.
26. Dr Y said in summary:
26.1. The consultation began with a review and the issuing of a repeat prescription.
There was a sense of relief at the passing of a crisis in Ms E's life, so they
hugged each other in an embrace. He said that he accepted what Ms E had
said in her statement that he had then locked the door, shut the blinds, and the

10
other conduct which she mentioned including the performing of thrusting
motions. He said he did not accept that Ms E was shocked or "numb" as she
had said, but accepted the conduct was unacceptable. He said that they then
composed themselves and talked about what had happened. In essence he
accepted there had been a breach of professional standards. He did not say that
he would need to write this into the notes. He said they also agreed to meet up
at Ms E's workplace and she provided the address.
26.2. Later that day he drove to the address which Ms E had told him was her work
address. In the course of doing so Ms E pulled up in her car. He said she had
given him the wrong address by mistake, so he got into her car and they drove
to her office. After meeting two colleagues he followed her to her office. He
accepted that it was likely he had shut the door, since he entered second. They
sat by an open sash window where they were close enough for their knees to
touch and some of the time held hands. They talked about what had happened.
They had liked each other but developments that morning were unexpected.
They discussed an ongoing relationship, and she said she had use of a family
member's cottage. They agreed to stay in touch, exchanged email addresses
which included Ms E's mobile phone number. During the meeting he lay back
on the floor, unzipped his trousers and suggested they have oral sex as Ms E
had asserted. He said he did not pull out or expose his penis.
26.3. In the course of cross examination when asked about the specifics of the events
in his consultation room, Dr Y said that there were "intermediate steps," about
which he declined to give details. When it was pointed out to him that these
had not been put to Ms E he said that he was not going to add to it either.
When asked about his evidence that he did not accept Ms E was "shocked or
numb," he said he did not believe this to be the case and that is why a
statement of facts was not agreed.

11
26.4. A similar situation arose with regard to his evidence as to what happened at
Ms E's office: when asked about the suggestion he made that there be oral sex
and whether Ms E had agreed to it, he said that he knew the answer but he was
not in a position to provide it.
26.5. Dr Y was then told by the Tribunal that by choosing not to provide full
disclosure in evidence and by putting Ms E in a position where she was not
asked about his understanding of events, he ran a risk that the Tribunal would
have to draw adverse inferences against him for his failure to provide relevant
evidence.
26.6. Both Counsel agreed that it would be appropriate for Dr Y to be provided with
advice as to his legal position. This occurred and Dr Y then provided more
information as to what had happened.
26.7. He said that the first encounter in his consultation room lasted about 25
minutes. The hug was really an embrace which was very prolonged and they
then kissed. His hand was up her back (against her skin); and her hand was up
his back but not inside his clothes. At some point he panicked. He shut the
curtains and closed the door. He said however, he did not want to have sex in
his consultation room, so instead he suggested Ms E bend over the bed and
they hugged over the bed, but the encounter was short and "fizzled out." Ms E
moaned in the course of the pelvic thrusting. There was he said no penile
stimulation or clitoral stimulation.
26.8. As regards the encounter at the office they met for approximately an hour.
After a long conversation Dr Y made the suggestion that Ms E perform oral
sex with him. He undid his trousers and then Ms E performed oral sex on him
for about a minute, after which he left to return to work.
26.9. He said there was a phone call which he initiated the next day; he described

12
this as "just catching up with each other." They had discussed the possibility
of a relationship the previous day and Dr Y said he was very sorry he had
allowed the situation to become "physical." He felt however that there was the
potential for a relationship.
26.10. There was a further telephone call when he again rang her about a week later.
They again discussed the relationship. By then Dr Y had formed the view that
the situation was "out of control", which he had really realised from the
beginning. He told Ms E that a relationship would not work. He considered
that she was feeling ambiguous about that possibility as well.
26.11. In respect of the meeting at the café over a year later, Dr Y felt there had been
a genuine misunderstanding. He had thought their interactions had been
mutual. In that conversation he understood she really was hurt, but he felt the
situation had been ambiguous at the time.
26.12. After the parties had met at the café, they had met by chance at a charity
fundraiser; they spoke for about 10 minutes about generalities. Dr Y did not
consider the meeting to be of significance.
Credibility issues:
27. Because Dr Y was not initially forthcoming in both his written and oral evidence the
Tribunal had to determine whether the additional disclosures were truthful.
28. The Tribunal has determined that the further information was indeed correct for the
following reasons:
28.1. The additional information obviously rendered the circumstances more
serious, as will be evident from the Tribunal's analysis below. It is hardly
likely that Dr Y would have fabricated a more serious account.
28.2. Dr Wisely was present when Dr Y made the additional disclosures to the
Tribunal. Dr Wisely said that the detail which had been provided by Dr Y to
him was consistent with the full account given by Dr Y to the Tribunal. This

13
gave the Tribunal more confidence in Dr Y's (fuller) account because there was
consistency in those disclosures.
28.3. That Ms E did not refer to the additional matters was because they were not
put to her. It appears this was because these details were not contained in
Dr Y's brief of evidence (as they should have been); Counsel (properly) cross
examined Ms E on the basis of the information in the brief, and not on the
basis of the further information with which the Tribunal was eventually
provided no doubt because Counsel was unaware of these details.
28.4. The Tribunal was also able to assess Dr Y's demeanour when giving his
evidence. He frankly made a number of concessions that were contrary to his
interests. Indeed as will be described more fully later in this decision, he was
able to analyse the events in detailed and balanced way which lent weight to
the credibility of his account.
29. Accordingly, the Tribunal finds that Dr Y's description of events. when finally given,
was accurate. It will however, be necessary later in this decision to comment on the
lack of prudence in not being candid to the Tribunal in the first instance.
Particular 1: breach of sexual boundary in a doctor/patient relationship during a
consultation, 10 March 2009:
30. The Tribunal finds that the events which occurred in Dr Y's consultation room were
not premeditated on his part. The Tribunal accepts his evidence that he felt he got on
well with this particular patient. She was from the UK as he was; they were both
health professionals of about the same age and had some similar experiences. She
was a "favourite patient", a person to whom he could relate positively. He agreed that
the rapidity of the events might have been explained by the fact that he had latent
feelings for her which he had not recognised a risk during consultations.
31. As far as Ms E is concerned, she said it could have been possible that she had flirted

14
with Dr Y; she said she found him to be a very charming and alluring man, and that
she was very flattered by what happened.
32. The Tribunal considers that the act of the doctor hugging his patient was a trigger for
what followed. It is hard to imagine a clinical consultation where hugging a patient of
the opposite sex does not cross a professional boundary, and it was a particularly
unwise step in these circumstances since it clearly led quickly to the subsequent
inappropriate interactions.
33. The situation quickly moved to the point where Dr Y recognised that appropriate
boundaries were being breached. This was evident after there had been some kissing
and cuddling, so he locked the door and closed the curtains. He obviously did not
want anyone to know what was happening. Then Dr Y asked Ms E to bend over the
table and he started to undertake thrusting motions. The Tribunal accepts this may
have been unexpected; Ms E's description that she was "numb" is an understandable
reaction to the situation. The Tribunal accepts she was shocked by what had
developed. Moreover, Dr Y locking the door could be intimidating and frightening
for a patient.
34. It is common ground that there was then a discussion about a breach of professional
standards – ie, there was an immediate acknowledgement on Dr Y's part that he had
acted inappropriately. There was a debate about whether he did or did not say he was
going to record this in the notes but that is not the primary point. What was
significant was what had occurred.
35. In terms of the Medical Council's guidelines, "Sexual Boundaries in a Doctor/Patient
Relationship" there was a "sexual transgression," namely inappropriate touching of a
patient that was of a sexual nature short of sexual violation.
36. On that basis, the first particular is clearly established.
Particular 2: breach of sexual boundaries in doctor/patient relationship at Ms E's place

15
of employment, 10 March 2009:
37. Although, as it transpires, there was no further consultation between Dr Y and Ms E
after 10 March 2009, there was no suggestion that by the time the parties met at Ms
E's office she should be regarded as a "former patient." She had not been referred by
Dr Y to another practitioner. But in any event as Dr Y properly accepted, the second
encounter arose from the first.
38. The Tribunal accepts the second meeting lasted for about an hour. There was an
intimate discussion wherein the parties explored whether they might engage in an
ongoing personal relationship. The Tribunal accepts that reference was made to them
using of a cottage about 20 minutes away from [ ], owned by one of Ms E's family
members. It also accepts that they agreed to stay in touch, exchanging email addresses
and a mobile phone number.
39. The Tribunal finds that there was then a brief encounter where Ms E was persuaded to
perform oral sex on Dr Y for about a minute. This ended fairly promptly, because Dr
Y had to go back to work.
40. This conduct was completely inappropriate. It amounted to sexual transgression
under the Medical Council guidelines. Sexual violation occurs in a doctor/patient
relationship when a doctor undertakes any form of sexual connection with a patient
(whether or not such is initiated by the patient). Here, the Tribunal finds the sexual
contact was initiated by Dr Y since he had recognised the possibility of sex in his
consultation room, avoided it there, but pursued Ms E to her work where he suggested
sexual activity. The sexual contact was a serious breach of sexual boundaries.
41. Particular 2 is clearly made out.
Conclusion as to professional misconduct:
42. Having reviewed the evidence and the submissions, the Tribunal announced at the
hearing that it was satisfied that each of the two particulars were properly established.
It stated that the circumstances constituted malpractice and the bringing of discredit to

16
the profession.
43. The Tribunal was concerned that the breaches raised significant concerns as to Dr Y's
judgment and self control. In two instances a patient who was vulnerable to the point
of requiring medication for depression and had other stressors in her life had to face
quite unexpected sexual overtures and physical contact from her doctor. The Tribunal
considers these events to be very serious. For the purposes of protecting the public,
and maintaining professional standards, discipline is obviously warranted. The charge
of professional misconduct is made out.
Lack of frankness:
44. The Tribunal has already commented on the unsatisfactory way in which Dr Y
presented his evidence.
45. A practitioner has a right not to give evidence – although as has been discussed in
previous cases there are risks in adopting this course.14
46. Subject to the privilege against self incrimination of a criminal offence, where a
practitioner elects to give evidence that practitioner is expected to give a complete
account of the relevant events, and to be truthful. If not, there is a risk of the
practitioner misleading the Tribunal and perhaps perjuring himself or herself.
47. Difficulties of this kind can all be avoided where the practitioner who elects to give
evidence does not omit relevant events. That principle applies to the provision of
written evidence to the Tribunal as well as oral evidence.
Evidence relevant to penalty:
48. Dr Y gave evidence relevant to penalty issues as follows:
48.1. He referred in his written statement to the conditions imposed by the Medical
Council, stating that his current employers were aware of these and that he had
complied with those conditions. It was understood the Medical Council had
14 See cases gathered at para 23.6 of Vatsyayann (355/Med10/152P) approved by Priestly J in Vatsyayann v PCC [2012]
NZHC 1138, at [46] and [47]

17
monitored the conditions by inquiries of the employers as well as an audit visit
to each of the workplaces so as to confirm adherence.
48.2. He also had two GP mentors, one male and one female, each of whom he met
four or more times per year; they had agreed to continue this role with this
until 2015.
48.3. He felt he had much better insight and awareness than was previously the case.
He felt that it had been an out of character incident, and assured the Tribunal
there would be no repeat.
48.4. In his oral evidence Dr Y agreed that Ms E would have felt powerless by the
events that occurred. He accepted there had been an unusual intensity on his
part which had caused distress to her.
48.5. Asked how he would react if he was in a stressful situation again, he told the
Tribunal that he was now more wary of patients. He felt he had learned a very
painful lesson. He had reflected carefully on what happened and realised that
it was up to him and not the patient to control a given situation. He felt his
guard was probably down because he was caring for a fellow professional; a
common professional background could blur the fact that the person involved
was actually a patient. A corollary of this was that a practitioner would need to
be wary of "shop talk in the consultation room." He also stated that he
intensely regretted what had occurred; the events had frightened him. He felt
he now had better peer support from a psychiatrist and mentors.
48.6. He had initially thought it would be difficult to comply with the Medical
Council conditions including the requirement to display a chaperone notice.
But he then realised he enjoyed practising medicine; this was more important
than any issue of status and it had made him more immune to vanity or flattery.
48.7. 20 references were produced from professional colleagues (nurses and doctors)

18
who have worked closely with Dr Y in a variety of professional contexts. The
writers were all aware of the present circumstances. They all spoke highly of
his rapport with patients, experience and competence as a doctor.
49. Dr Wisely also gave evidence to the Tribunal. He advised:
49.1. He had diagnosed Dr Y as suffering from a mixed anxiety and depressive
disorder, for which he prescribed Fluoxetine on a modest dose.
49.2. He considered the events were "very much out of character", and that it was
apparent Dr Y was under stress at the time with very significant stressors in his
life which he explained. He considered that Dr Y had been able to address the
stresses and issues he faced in an appropriate way.
49.3. He was also of the view that Dr Y had analytically examined his own conduct
in a way that he felt showed good insight, without reticence. In his view, Dr Y
was "a very low risk" to the public and could practise medicine safely and
effectively.
49.4. He amplified these matters in his oral evidence. He felt that Dr Y was
definitely motivated to clean up the mess and move on. He felt that Dr Y was
now being "painfully honest."
Penalty submissions:
50. It was submitted by the Director:
50.1. The Tribunal should impose a six months suspension from practice to reflect
the seriousness of Dr Y's conduct; the Medical Council conditions on practice
should be formalised with parallel Tribunal conditions for a period of three
years, and that two further conditions should be imposed (the undertaking of a
SMAT assessment, and a course as to professional boundaries); a censure and
costs order should also be imposed.
50.2. The relevant legal cases relating to sentencing were referred to – these are

19
considered below.
50.3. Dr Y had sexually exploited the patient and propositioned her, contrary to
Medical Council guidelines. It was submitted that he was apparently
overcome by sexual desire for his patient; and that his conduct presented
serious public safety concerns. The Tribunal might wish to consider the
possibility that stress impacts on Dr Y's behaviour.
50.4. Although there are numerous Tribunal cases concerning sexual misconduct,
this was a case where there was unusually intensive sexual behaviour. In
previous cases the Tribunal had generally imposed a cancellation order for
sexual misconduct (although that was not considered a proportionate outcome
in this case) or suspension.15
50.5. It was submitted that rehabilitation objectives could be met by the proposed
conditions, but that a six months suspension order was necessary to mark the

Legal principles – penalty:
52. There is a convenient summary of sentencing principles in Katamat v PCC:19
"[49] In Roberts v Professional Conduct Committee, Collins J identified the
following eight factors as being relevant whenever the Tribunal is
determining an appropriate penalty. They are which penalty:
(1) most appropriately protects the public and deters others;
(2) facilitates the Tribunal's "important" role in setting
professional standards;
(3) punishes the practitioner;
(4) allows for the rehabilitation of the health practitioner;
(5) promotes consistency with penalties in similar cases;
(6) reflects the seriousness of the misconduct;
(7) is the least restrictive penalty appropriate in the circumstances;
and
(8) looked at overall, is the penalty which is "fair, reasonable and
proportionate in the circumstances".
[50] In Patel v Dentists Disciplinary Tribunal, regarding the decision to de-
register the practitioner specifically, Randerson J held that:
… the task of the Tribunal is to balance the nature and gravity
of the offences and their bearing on the dentist's fitness to
practise against the need for removal and its consequences to
the individual: Dad v General Dental Council at 1543. As the
Privy Council further observed: [in Dad]
Such consequences [cancellation] can properly be
regarded as inevitable where the nature or gravity of the
offence indicates that a dentist is unfit to practise, that
rehabilitation is unlikely and that he must be suspended or
have his name erased from the register. In cases of that
kind greater weight must be given to the public interest and
to the need to maintain public confidence in the profession
than to the consequences of the imposition of the penalty to
the individual.
[51] Similarly in A v Professional Conduct Committee, Keane J derives the
following five principles from the Privy Council speeches in Taylor v
19 [2012] NZHC 1633, 21 December 2012, per Williams J

23
General Medical Council:
First, the primary purpose of cancelling or suspending
registration is to protect the public, but that 'inevitably imports
some punitive element'. Secondly, to cancel is more punitive than
to suspend and the choice between the two turns on what is
proportionate. Thirdly, to suspend implies the conclusion that
cancellation would have been disproportionate. Fourthly,
suspension is most apt where there is 'some condition affecting
the practitioner's fitness to practise which may or may not be
amenable to cure'. Fifthly, and perhaps only implicitly,
suspension ought not to be imposed simply to punish.
[52] Keane J continued, affirming the importance of considerations of
rehabilitation:
… the Tribunal cannot ignore the rehabilitation of the
practitioner: B v B (HC Auckland, HC 4/92, 6 April 1993)
Blanchard J. Moreover, as was said in Giele v The General
Medical Council [2005] EWHC 2143, though '… the
maintenance of public confidence … must outweigh the interests
of the individual doctor', that is not absolute – 'the existence of
the public interest in not ending the career of a competent doctor
will play a part.'
[53] In summary, the case law reveals that several factors will be relevant
to assessing what penalty is appropriate in the circumstances. Some
factors, such as the need to protect the public and to maintain
professional standards, are more intuitive in their application. Others,
such as the seriousness of offending and consistency with past cases,
are more concrete and capable of precise evaluation. Of all the factors
discussed, the primary factor will be what penalty is required to protect
the public and deter similar conduct. The need to punish the
practitioner can be considered, but is of secondary importance. The
objective seriousness of the misconduct, the need for consistency with
past cases, the likelihood of rehabilitation and the need to impose the
least restrictive penalty that is appropriate will all be relevant to the
inquiry. It bears repeating, however, that the overall decision is
ultimately one involving an exercise of discretion."
Penalty – discussion:
53. The Tribunal finds that the following are the aggravating features of this matter:
53.1. The first particular involved a serious sexual transgression. As Dr Y frankly
conceded, there was an unusual intensity with regard to his actions which
caused distress to Ms E.
53.2. There was an almost immediate recognition that sexual boundaries had been
crossed. Notwithstanding that fact the situation moved relatively quickly to a

24
second encounter where there was an even more serious breach, a sexual
violation. It is particularly concerning that the second incident occurred in the
face of apparent insight at the time of the first encounter.
53.3. Ms E was a vulnerable patient. To Dr Y's knowledge, she had had a
relationship breakdown and was in very difficult financial circumstances; she
had moved recently to [ ], which had created added stress. As a result of the
stressors in her life she was on anti-depressants. Although Dr Y saw Ms E as a
health practitioner, the primary relationship was one of doctor and patient.
There was a significant power imbalance that Dr Y failed to recognise.
53.4. The Tribunal has some concern at the rapidity of the events. Whilst Dr Y may
well have been attracted to Ms E prior to 10 March, the Tribunal accepts that
he did not intend sexual activity on that occasion; the rapidity of what occurred
has to be seen in that context. Regrettably, there was an element of self
gratification in the conduct. The Tribunal also observes that it was unwise for
the parties to have hugged and embraced. This led all too quickly and easily to
the subsequent conduct.
53.5. There was initially a lack of frankness in Dr Y's evidence. As the Tribunal has
already commented, it is totally unacceptable to provide an incomplete brief of
evidence to the Tribunal, and then refrain from explaining the full context, for
a time. It is unclear why this problem arose. However, common sense
eventually prevailed; the Tribunal was able to obtain a more complete
understanding of the circumstances, and indeed this satisfied the Tribunal that
the second encounter was more serious than the first.
54. There are the following mitigating factors:
54.1. Dr Wisely gave detailed evidence to the Tribunal from his perspective as a
treating psychiatrist. His evidence was credible and reliable. The Tribunal
accepts Dr Wisely's evidence that the conduct was "very much out of

25
character", and was catalysed by the stress which he was suffering at the time
– the details of which he explained. These issues were compounded by low
self esteem. In summary, Dr Wisely's evidence suggested that Dr Y is not a
predator and there was an element of vulnerability on his part because of his
circumstances. This is not a defence but it is a factor which the Tribunal
should take into account at the penalty stage.
54.2. A related issue is that there is a minimal risk of recurrence. There is no
evidence of any further difficulties since 2009. Dr Y has reacted appropriately
to the conditions which have been put in place, recognising the importance of
the restrictions which have been imposed. The Tribunal is also satisfied that
the process itself has and will act as a significant disincentive for any
repetition.
54.3. Dr Y's admission of guilt was candid.20 Once he gave the fuller explanation,
he did not attempt to qualify the seriousness of his position or suggest that it
was in any way excusable. Related to this aspect is his significant
demonstration of insight as to the inappropriateness of his conduct.
54.4. He has appropriately sought out help, although not until August 2010. From
then on he has been assisted by psychotherapy and mentoring which has
assisted his rehabilitation.
54.5. Dr Y apologised to Ms E the day following the encounter, and again at the café
conversation (although it appears the circumstances of that meeting were not
ideal and there was some misunderstanding between the parties). His position
was formalised with an appropriate written apology to the complainant in
March 2013 and again when giving evidence.
20 Paras 12 and 20 of his brief

26
54.6. As already commented, 20 significant and positive references have been
produced from professional colleagues, all of which confirm that Dr Y is
in all other respects a competent practitioner; many expressed an opinion that
the conduct could properly be regarded as out of character.
Other cases:
55. The Tribunal has been invited to consider a significant number of other cases, all of
which have been carefully reviewed.
56. As to the decisions referred to by the Director:
56.1. In Tamma, the Tribunal imposed an order of 18 months suspension followed
by conditions on return to practice. The Director fairly conceded that the facts
of that case were more serious than in the present case. The Tribunal agrees
with this. While in Tamma the doctor used an obvious power imbalance
against a vulnerable patient who could not speak English, Dr Y did not
recognise the power imbalance in his treatment of Ms E, a fellow health
professional. Regrettably, both instances used this power imbalance to seek
self-gratification.
56.2. The second decision referred to by the Director was S, which involved a
psychologist crossing professional boundaries in a variety of respects with his
patient, on multiple occasions. A particular feature of that case was the
significant vulnerability of the patient who had been a victim of sexual abuse
throughout her childhood. Again, the Tribunal considers that case to have very
different features from the present one.
57. Of the cases referred to by Counsel for Dr Y (all of which were reviewed carefully)
the decision which is of most assistance is Gray. In that case there was a sexual
relationship between a doctor and his patient for some four months. Factors which the
Tribunal took into account were:

27
57.1. The doctor's conduct was not predatory, and should accordingly be
distinguished from other cases where that characteristic was a feature.
57.2. The doctor had a large number of stressors in his own life, and had been seeing
a psychiatrist, which supported a finding that the doctor was to some extent
vulnerable.
57.3. The community within which the doctor practised was aware of the events, as
was evident from various letters placed before the Tribunal.
57.4. Positive evidence was presented to the Tribunal by the doctor of the steps
which the doctor had taken to ensure the safety of his medical practice.
57.5. The doctor had practised safely in the three and a half years since the
complaint against him was made.
57.6. Whilst the Tribunal in that case had some concerns regarding the doctor's
insight and overall judgment, it was particularly influenced by the fact the
doctor had been practising safely for some three and a half years since the
events giving rise to the charge occurred, and had put in place a number of
measures to ensure that he practised safely. The Tribunal also referred to the
fact that the community and the practice within which he was currently
practising could be re-assured of his commitment to avoid re-offending. The
Tribunal determined that as a matter of fairness it should take into account the
personal rehabilitative efforts he had undertaken, and the steps he had taken
into improve and ensure the safety of his general practice. Balancing all those
factors the Tribunal censured the practitioner, fined him $7,500.00 (the
maximum fine was $20,000.00), imposed a sentence of suspension for six
months but suspended that for three years, and ordered him to pay 50% of the
costs involved. In addition, it placed conditions on his practice; there was no
issue as to publication of the doctor's name.

28
58. Whilst the circumstances of that case were certainly more serious than in the present
(the sexual conduct took place over a period of months and gave rise to a finding of
"disgraceful conduct"), there are some parallels in the mitigating factors. To that
extent, the decision is of assistance.
59. Counsel for Dr Y referred to three particular decisions involving a suspension (G,
McDonald and Patel), suggesting that they were more serious cases justifying a more
serious penalty than in this case. Although not direct comparators, each of those
decisions were very serious; furthermore the practitioners in those cases could not
invoke the range of mitigating factors which arise in the present case.
60. After reviewing all cases, the Tribunal considers that the options for it are to order a
short period of suspension for deterrent purposes and impose conditions for
rehabilitation purposes; alternatively, to impose a fine for deterrent purposes as well
as conditions. If it were to conclude that suspension was appropriate, the Tribunal
would then be required to consider the possibility of suspension, as advocated for Dr
Y.
Conclusion as to penalty:
61. The circumstances of the present case are very unusual. Whilst the Tribunal cannot
but be concerned by the mix of aggravating factors summarised above, it must also
recognise the strength of the mitigating factors. Particularly important is the
practitioner's insight, and his willingness to adhere to restrictions designed to protect
public health and safety. Also important are the strong references which recognise Dr
Y is in many respects competent and reliable.
62. Accordingly, given both a sexual transgression as well as a sexual violation soon after,
the appropriate outcome in this case is to impose a significant fine of $25,000.00, in
order to make it plain to Dr Y and to other health professionals that the conduct
reviewed in this case is viewed very seriously indeed by the Tribunal. By a narrow

29
margin, an order of suspension is not in the present case appropriate.
63. There will also be conditions on practice, as outlined below. The Tribunal regards the
imposition of conditions by it for a period of three years as appropriate, to reinforce
the fact that there must be Tribunal ordered protections in place to re-assure the public
that in circumstances such as the present health and safety of patients is a paramount
consideration for the Tribunal.
64. Having regard to the various sentencing objectives outlined in the Roberts decision,
the Tribunal considers these orders will:
64.1. ensure the protection of the public;
64.2. maintain standards;
64.3. support the practitioner's rehabilitation;
64.4. ensure its orders are consistent with other decisions;
64.5. impose orders which sit correctly in the spectrum of sentencing options;
64.6. ensure that the least restrictive penalties are imposed.
65. Standing back, the Tribunal is satisfied that the penalty imposed is fair, reasonable
and proportionate.

Legal principles – non-publication of name:
76. Section 95 of the Act governs issues of non-publication of name. It relevantly
provides:
"1. Section 95(1) every hearing of the Tribunal must be held in public
unless the Tribunal orders otherwise under this section or unless
section 97 applies.
2. If, after having regard to the interests of any person (including, without
limitation, the privacy of any complainant) and to the public interest,
the Tribunal is satisfied that it is desirable to do so, it may (on
application by any of their parties or on its own initiative) make any
one or more of the following orders:
(a) An order that the whole or any part of a hearing must be held in
private:
(b) An order prohibiting the publication of any report or account of
any part of a hearing, whether held in public or in private:
(c) An order prohibiting the publication of the whole or any part of
any books, papers, or documents produced at a hearing.

35
(d) An order prohibiting the publication of the name, or any
particulars of the affairs, of any person."
77. In many previous decisions,32 the Tribunal has evaluated the following public interest
factors:
77.1. Openness and transparency of disciplinary proceedings.33
77.2. Accountability of the disciplinary process.34
77.3. Public interest in knowing the identity of a health practitioner charged with a
disciplinary offence.35
77.4. Importance of freedom of speech and the right enshrined in section 14,
New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990.36
77.5. Unfairly impugning other health practitioners.37
78. Also relevant is the statement made by Pankhurst J in A v Director of Proceedings:
“[F]ollowing an adverse disciplinary finding more weighty factors are
necessary before permanent suppression will be desirable. This, I think,
follows from the protective nature of the jurisdiction. Once an adverse finding
has been made, the probability must be that public interest considerations will
require that the name of the practitioner be published in a preponderance of
cases. Thus, the statutory test of what is “desirable” is necessarily flexible.
Prior to the substantive hearing of the charges the balance in terms of what is
desirable may incline in favour of the private interests of the practitioner.
After the hearing, by which time the evidence is out and findings have been
made, what is desirable may well be different, the more so where professional
misconduct has been established.”38
79. In B v B, supra, the Court held at page 99:
"In normal course where a professional person appears before the disciplinary
tribunal and is found guilty of an offence, that person should expect that an
order preventing publication of his or her name will not be made. That will
especially be so where the offence found to be proved, or admitted, is
sufficiently serious to justify striking off or suspension from practice. But
where the orders made by a disciplinary tribunal in relation to future practice
of the defendant directed towards that person's rehabilitation and there is no

Director of Proceedings v I [2004] NZAR 635
34 Director of Proceedings v Nursing Council [1999] 3 NZLR 360

5 December 2001, HC Auckland AP21-SW01)
36 R v Liddell, supra and Lewis v Wilson & Horton Ltd, supra; Gravatt v Coroners Court [2013] NZHC 390, [38] & [39].

suppression to avoid suspicion falling on other members of a profession.

striking off or suspension but rather, as here, a decision that practice may
continue, there is much to be said for the view that publication of the

80. In Anderson v PCC (High Court, Wellington CIV-2008-485-1646, 14 November
2008) Gendall J stated:
"[36] Private interests will include the health interests of a practitioner,
matters that may affect a family and their wellbeing, and rehabilitation.
Correspondingly, interests such as protection of the public,
maintenance of professional standards, both openness and
'transparency' and accountability of the disciplinary process, the basic
value of freedom to receive and impart information, the public interest
knowing the identity of a practitioner found guilty of professional

[37] Those factors were also referred to at some length in the Tribunal. Of

practitioner to be punitive but its purpose is to protect and advance the
public interest by ensuring that it is informed of the disciplinary
process and of practitioners who may be guilty of malpractice or
professional misconduct. It reflects also the principles of openness of
such proceedings, and freedom to receive and impart information."
81. It is also necessary to have regard to the proportionality principle referred to by
Baragwanath J in J v Director of Proceedings (17 October 2006, CIV-2006-404-2188,
paragraph [71]).
Discussion – non-publication of name:
82. The following factors favour publication:
82.1. Accountability: the Tribunal accepts the Director's submission that public
accountability is one way in which standards are maintained. As it was put, it
is important that Dr Y and other general practitioners understand that one of
the consequences of serious misconduct is that public and professional peers
become aware of that misconduct; that requires their identification. This factor
is an important consideration in this case given the seriousness of the
misconduct involved.

37
82.2. At a more general level, the important principles of open justice which have
been explored on many occasions, and which are summarised for example by
Gendall J in Anderson, are entitled to weight.
82.3. The right of patients to know that their doctor has faced a professional
disciplinary charge involving breaches of boundaries. Whilst the Tribunal
accepts that the imposition of conditions, and the other checks and balances
which have been referred to will in part achieve this, these factors are not a
complete answer; nor would a condition that if asked the relevant information
would be provided to a patient while such possibilities as these may go some
distance to ensuring some patients are properly informed they would not
ensure all patients are properly informed. All patients are entitled to be
informed as to issues such as the present without having to ask. This principle
is entitled to weight in this case, especially as Dr Y works at a number of
medical centres.
The entitlement to know was a factor given particular weight by Laurenson J in
F v Medical Practitioners Disciplinary Tribunal;39 the Tribunal considers that
it is a matter which should be carefully considered in the present instance.
82.4 It is also a feature of open justice that not only do patients have a right to
know, but so does the public generally including other members of the
profession. Whilst it is clear that there are some practitioners who are aware
of Dr Y's difficulties – as is evidenced by the references – this principle goes
wider than the disclosure that has occurred to this point. It is a factor which
needs to be carefully considered.
83. In favour of an order of non-publication are the following factors:
83.1. The mental health issues which were discussed fully by Dr Wisley in his

statement and in his oral evidence.40 However, the Tribunal is impressed with
the supports which Dr Y now has in place to address these issues, including
appropriate medication. The existence of peer reviews and the fact that
colleagues are aware of the circumstances suggest there is a significant degree
of support for Dr Y which the Tribunal is confident will help mitigate the
possibility of psychiatric illness. The Tribunal is not satisfied that the mental
health issues are such that publication would cause irreparable harm, as
suggested in Dr Wisely’s statement of evidence.
83.2. [ ]
83.3. The Tribunal accepts that Dr Y's reputation would be harmed by publication.
Unfortunately, that is an inevitable consequence in practically all cases that
come before the Tribunal where a charge is made out. It is not a factor which
is entitled to significant weight, where the misconduct is serious.
83.4. Delay has been raised as a factor. The circumstances occurred four and a half
years ago. This is a factor which is entitled to some weight, but it is not
determinative as it was in the case of C.
84. Standing back the evidence shows that Dr Y is particularly well supported, as just
explained. He has strong references, and is a competent doctor who is committed to
ensuring he can maintain his commitment to his profession. He is well motivated.
The Tribunal does not therefore consider that this is a case where rehabilitation would
be impeded by publication. Moreover, the Tribunal does not consider that the
publication of his name will adversely affect those practices where he works,
particularly as Dr Y’s need for a chaperone in them is already clearly displayed.

Rehabilitation is an important objective in this case – that is why the Tribunal has
decided not to order suspension. But the Tribunal is satisfied that rehabilitation will
not be compromised.
85. Against the various privacy considerations have to be weighed factors such as the
protection of the public, the maintenance of professional standards and the
accountability of the disciplinary process, as well as the public interest in knowing the
identity of a practitioner against whom a charge is established.
86. After considering all factors, the Tribunal is not satisfied that it is desirable to make a
permanent order of non-publication.
87. In the authorities summarised above, reference is made to the proportionality
principle: J v Director of Proceedings. The Tribunal's overall assessment is that
publication of name together with all other penalty outcomes results in a proportionate
response to the established charges.
88. Accordingly, the interim order of non-publication of name will now be discharged
according to the timetable outlined below.
